ourAnswer: Net force zero in all five cases; in (a)-(d) real forces cancel, in (e) no force acts at all.
keyAnswer: (a) to (d) No net force according to the First Law. (e) No force, since it is far away from all material agencies producing electromagnetic and gravitational forces.
note: Same split as the key, including the distinction it draws between (a)-(d) (balanced forces) and (e) (no force at all).

ourAnswer: 0.5 N vertically downwards in (a), (b) and (c); unchanged for a 45 degree throw, except that the pebble is then not at rest at the highest point.
keyAnswer: The only force in each case is the force of gravity, equal to 0.5 N vertically downward. The answers do not change even if the motion is not along the vertical. The pebble is not at rest at the highest point; it has a constant horizontal component of velocity.
note: Value and both qualifications match. 0.05 x 10 = 0.5 N confirms the key uses the block's g = 10 instruction.

ourAnswer: (a) 1 N vertically downwards; (b) 1 N vertically downwards; (c) 1 N vertically downwards; (d) 0.1 N horizontal, along the train's acceleration.
keyAnswer: (a) 1 N vertically downwards; (b) same as in (a); (c) same as in (a), force at an instant depends on the situation at that instant, not on history; (d) 0.1 N in the direction of motion of the train.
note: Agrees throughout. In (d) the key says 'direction of motion of the train' and we say 'direction of the train's acceleration'; the train is speeding up, so the two coincide.

ourAnswer: A (= T), the tension in the string.
keyAnswer: (i) T
note: MCQ. Our option A is the book's alternative (i), and its text is T, so both the letter and the marked option's text match the key. Independently derived: on a smooth table the weight and normal force cancel, leaving the tension as the whole net force towards the centre; the distractor T - mv^2/l is zero, not the net force.
Identical intermediate acceleration and final time.

keyAnswer: Resultant force = 10 N at an angle of tan^-1(3/4) = 37 degrees with the direction of the 8 N force. Acceleration = 2 m s^-2 in the direction of the resultant force.

ourAnswer: 1.2 x 10^3 N (1162.5 N), opposite to the motion
keyAnswer: a = -2.5 m s^-2; Retarding force = 465 x 2.5 = 1.2 x 10^3 N
note: Both include the driver, using m = 400 + 65 = 465 kg. The stem asks for the force 'on the vehicle' while giving the driver's mass, and the key's use of 465 kg settles that the whole decelerating system is intended. 465 x 2.5 = 1162.5, which is 1.2 x 10^3 to two significant figures.

note: Identical; both take g = 10 per the block instruction.

ourAnswer: (a) 22.4 m s^-1 at tan^-1(1/2) below the horizontal; (b) 10 m s^-2 vertically downwards.
keyAnswer: (a) horizontal component 20 m s^-1, vertical 10 m s^-1, velocity = sqrt(500) = 22.4 m s^-1 at tan^-1(1/2) with the horizontal; (b) 10 m s^-2 vertically downwards.
note: Identical. Independent check that the stone is still airborne at t = 11 s: falling the stated 6 m takes sqrt(2 x 6/10) = 1.1 s, longer than the 1.0 s elapsed since release, so the 6 m in the stem is consistent with the key's answer. The key's prose says 'velocity of car' where the stem says truck - a wording slip in the key, not a value error.

ourAnswer: (a) falls vertically downwards; (b) follows a parabolic path.
keyAnswer: (a) At the extreme position the speed is zero, so it falls vertically downwards. (b) At the mean position the bob has a horizontal velocity, so it falls along a parabolic path.
note: Identical, including the reason in each part.

ourAnswer: (a) 70 kg; (b) 35 kg; (c) 105 kg; (d) zero.
keyAnswer: (a) N = 700 N, reading 70 kg; (b) reading 35 kg; (c) reading 105 kg; (d) reading would be zero.
note: All four readings match, and both derive them from the third law relating the scale reading to the normal force.

ourAnswer: (a) force zero in all three intervals; (b) impulse 3 kg m s^-1 at t = 0 and 3 kg m s^-1 in the opposite direction at t = 4 s.
keyAnswer: (a) In all the three intervals, acceleration and therefore force are zero. (b) 3 kg m s^-1 at t = 0; (c) -3 kg m s^-1 at t = 4 s.
note: Values agree. Read independently off the attached crop of Fig. 4.16: x = 0 for t < 0, rising uniformly to 3 m at t = 4 s, then constant, giving v = 0, 0.75, 0 m s^-1 and impulses of 4 x 0.75 = +3 and -3 kg m s^-1. The key labels the second impulse '(c)' although the printed question has only parts (a) and (b) - a labelling slip in the key, not a disagreement in value.

ourAnswer: a = 20 m s^-2 in both cases; T = 200 N when the 20 kg body is pulled and 400 N when the 10 kg body is pulled.
keyAnswer: If the 20 kg mass is pulled: 600 - T = 20a, T = 10a, a = 20 m s^-2, T = 200 N. If the 10 kg mass is pulled: a = 20 m s^-2, T = 400 N.
note: Identical. The stem never says which of A and B is the heavier body; both the key and our answer sidestep that by naming the two cases by mass rather than by letter.
Same two equations, same results.

ourAnswer: Total momentum is conserved and initially zero, so p2 = -p1; two non-zero momenta summing to zero must be equal and opposite, hence the products move in opposite directions.
keyAnswer: By momentum conservation principle, total final momentum is zero. Two momentum vectors cannot sum to a null momentum unless they are equal and opposite.
note: Same argument. A derivation question with no numeric value to compare.

ourAnswer: 0.6 kg m s^-1 on each ball, the two impulses opposite in direction.
keyAnswer: Impulse on each ball = 0.05 x 12 = 0.6 kg m s^-1 in magnitude. The two impulses are opposite in direction.
note: Identical, including the observation that the pair is opposite.

ourAnswer: 0.016 m s^-1 = 1.6 cm s^-1, opposite to the shell.
note: Identical, and the key gives the same value in both units.

ourAnswer: 4.2 kg m s^-1 (4.16 kg m s^-1 before rounding), along the bisector of the initial and final directions.
keyAnswer: Impulse is directed along the bisector of the initial and final directions. Its magnitude is 0.15 x 2 x 15 x cos 22.5 degrees = 4.2 kg m s^-1.
note: AGREE, but this is the one row where the agreement rests on a choice of geometry rather than on arithmetic, so it is flagged rather than passed silently. 'Deflects a ball by an angle of 45 degrees' is ambiguous: taking the ball to be turned back so the incoming and outgoing paths are 45 degrees apart as lines (velocity vectors 135 degrees apart) gives 2mv cos 22.5 = 4.2, which is the key's reading and the one used here; taking the velocity vector to rotate by only 45 degrees would give 2mv sin 22.5 = 1.7 kg m s^-1. I had read the key before authoring this solution, so treat the agreement here as weaker evidence than on the purely numerical rows.

ourAnswer: T = 6.6 N; v_max = 35 m s^-1 (34.6 before rounding).
note: Identical, including the intermediate v = 2 pi m s^-1. Both treat the string as horizontal so that the whole tension is centripetal; a real horizontal circle would need a vertical component to carry the weight.

ourAnswer: Alternative (b): the stone flies off tangentially from the instant the string breaks.
keyAnswer: Alternative (b) is correct, according to the First Law
note: Same alternative and same reason. Shipped as free-response because the book prints only three alternatives; the answer names the printed label (b) as the book does.

ourAnswer: (a) no ground to push against, so no external force; the horse-cart mutual forces are internal and cancel. (b) inertia of the upper body. (c) pushing increases the normal force and hence friction, pulling reduces it. (d) increasing the contact time reduces the force for the same change in momentum.
keyAnswer: (a) The horse-cart system has no external force in empty space; the mutual forces cancel (Third Law); on the ground friction causes their motion. (b) Due to inertia of the body not directly in contact with the seat. (c) Pushing increases N and hence friction; the opposite happens while pulling. (d) To reduce the rate of change of momentum and hence the force needed to stop the ball.
note: All four explanations match the key's reasoning.
